en: “The lion of humankind,
Almambet has died,” say, and leave.
If I miss the appointed day,
Turn back without going to Beijing.
“My champion Almambet has died,”
Tell the twelve khans behind us!
The reason I speak my testament:
There is a road to Beijing
From which those who go do not return.
There is a road to Beijing
From which those who encounter it do not turn back.
There is a road to Beijing
With a pit dug in it.
There is a road to Beijing
With an assembled army.
If you fall into Chinese hands,
There is brine they have set boiling.
Farewell, my blue-maned Khan Manas!”
As he spoke these words,
Khan Manas was pleased with his speech,
He would not spare his own life,
For a lion like Almambet.
“My Almambet, my red spear's banner,
Who came from his people without looking back,
My gift that came from the Chinese!
My Almambet, does not one die when death is due?
The torment laid upon his neck—
Must not a young man endure it?
Against Beijing where Iskender never trod,
Swing and stretch your spear for me.
Reach Beijing where no one goes,
And wreak havoc there for me.
Scatter the Chinese herds for me.
Heed my words, my champion;
Open the Kyrgyz people's road for me.
To scout in Beijing,
To scout and gather news,
Let me choose from the horses for you.
Take my steed Kartküröng.
If your provisions are too few,
Pour my blood into a leather flask and take it.
Take a valley where horses may be hidden;
Without feeling shame, to Beijing
Take your prince beside you.
From the twelve Kyrgyz lineages,
Let me gather everyone;
Let me send them past in a line.
Choose and mark a companion in spear-fighting.
The Chinese realm's Beijing
Is a place of fearful reputation.
Choose a companion to stand beside you.”
Then your Almambet started in alarm.
“My peerless generous lord, what are you saying?
The peoples of your twelve khans,
When you gather them all,
What wish could I fulfill?
Give me a companion who is my equal—
Let me go with Syrgak.
With golden tea-urns and cheap tea,
There is no city like Samarkand.
When charging an enemy in spear-fighting,
To stand and fight,
There is no youth like Syrgak.
For young Syrgak, the leopard,
The whole Kyrgyz people together,
And my own wretched head, be a sacrifice!
Give me Syrgak; I shall take him,
And then I shall reconnoiter!
Brave Syrgak never rests upon his elbows,
Never takes even a brief sleep.
Light for a horse, just right for a colt,
Sleepless and watchful against the foe,
He throws the whole world into turmoil.
Brave Syrgak, dear to me,
Never draws back his leveled spear,
Never slinks away from a ravine,
Never brings distress upon an enemy.
If foes appear surrounding him on every side,
He never slips away and turns back.
I shall not return without reaching Beijing.
Do not make me fret so much;
I shall not part from my champion Syrgak.
Syrgak's strength suffices for the world.
Related to you through his father,
You are children of two brothers.
The brim of my black felt hat—
May he be safe, may he not die,
My Syrgak, whenever it may be.
Khan Ulak and Khan Jakyp,
These two are brothers.
If I live, I shall scout Beijing.
Khan Ulak's Syrgak
I regard as I do you.
At Beijing with its fearful wonders,
I shall shout and level my spear.
Against the Chinese foes who fight us,
I shall make Syrgak my support.
If my appointed death comes, let me die.
The Chinese whom lions dare not approach—
This year I shall see their strength.”
When your Almambet had said this,
Khan Manas spoke:
“Farewell then, leopard.
All the gear is packed,
He was sixty horse-years old;
It is loaded on Kartküröng.”
Manas and Chubak, the two lions,
Both remained at the baggage camp.
Among horses, the swift one has a mottled head;
Almambet and Syrgak, their names in harmony,
Mounted and set out to scout.
Sparing none of their prayerful words,
Goshawk Manas and brave Chubak,
Raising both their hands,
With tears welling from their eyes,
Murmured their blessings.
Almambet and Syrgak, the two lions,
Mounted without delay,
And entered the road without turning back.
Khan Manas watched them,
His heart burning with deep sorrow.
Almambet and Syrgak, the two lions,
Headed toward Beijing's heart,
Scouting the Chinese lands.
Khan Manas and Chubak together
Remained on Tal-Choku.
Azizkan's Almambet,
With dark-maned Syrgak beside him,
Along the road he knew,
Along springs flowing through valleys,
Through mountains with high passes,
Past towering cliffs,
With no grass to pluck,
With no water to give a drop,
Where heat never left the ground,
Where overhead, circling,
No winged bird flew across,
Through those far-flung lands
They traveled without stopping or looking back.
They rode far, sparing no horses.
Much thought left him dazed.
To Zhangyryk’s Zhar-Kyya,
A winding track where dragons do not go,
To the hollow of Teshik-Tash,
Along the whitening plain,
When they drew near,
Brave Syrgak behind him
Looked all around.
In one place stood a marksman,
Aiming straight, ready to shoot.
In another place stood a dragon,
Ready to bewitch and suck them in.
When Syrgak looked to one side,
A snow leopard stood ready to seize him.
A tiger stood crouched for a spring,
A lion ready to charge upon him.
When he saw all this,
Young Syrgak thought:
“My dear eyes, bright as Venus—
Has he come to have them gouged out?
To dragons and snakes,
Deceiving me into scouting,
If Almambet wishes,
Has he come to have me swallowed?
Sooner or later I am dead;
I have followed your Almambet here.
If the dragon draws in a breath,
I shall slaughter it without mercy.
If the tiger comes and attacks,
I shall put it to death.
Their fortified defenses,
I shall shatter and pass through.
Almambet ahead of me—
I shall pursue and catch him.
Spilling his blood here,
I shall turn back and leave!”
Taking his equipment and making ready,
Fierce brave Syrgak,
With steel strapped at his side,
Rushed on breathlessly,
Close behind Sarala ahead,
Riding on his very heels.
Seeing Syrgak's expression,
Almambet, born a mighty beast, thought:
“If the lookout should see us,
Now the Chinese infidels will see us.
If my Syrgak behaves like this,
He will be the utter ruin of me.
To the Chinese lying in wait,
He will give cause for suspicion.”
Thinking this, Almambet
Turned Sarala's head.
A powder-flask and some powder,
Your Almambet drew out, rumbling.
A palmful of the powder
He struck against his palate.
Beating the saddle-bow,
Again and again with his whip,
Striking the stirrup,
Speaking in Kalmyk, rattling,
Speaking in Chinese, babbling,
Reciting the Chinese spells,
Almambet, who knew their arts,
Now recited incantations.
As Almambet recited incantations,
The dragon fled, hissing;
The marksman fled, sighing;
The tiger fled along the mountains;
The snow leopard fled along the cliffs.
The boar fled into the forest.
The spells shattered to pieces,
Faded away and vanished.
When he saw this magic,
He turned Sarala's head.
“Almambet, tell the truth,”
Syrgak pressed him there.
“You made a dream no sleeper could see.
When the dragon was about to swallow us,
You did something beyond human power, Almambet!
Tell me the honest truth.
If you do not tell your true secret,
I shall not obey you;
Even if I die, I shall not go to Beijing!”
“My champion Syrgak, listen.
Their short-hemmed robe—
When I wore it,
Never letting them out of my palm,
The Chinese, people of forty khans—
When I ruled them,
With no thought of becoming Kyrgyz,
For the Manzhuu and Chinese multitudes,
Building thick walls and making fortifications,
When I was their protecting wall,
In the Chinese realm's Beijing,
With a precious rank-button on my cap,
When I was their khan,
My lion-like waist bent:
‘He will conquer Beijing;
The Burut will bring about my ruin.’
In the Chinese book of records
Blue-maned Manas was depicted.
When they saw this,
The Chinese with rank-buttons on their caps,
Too frightened to eat,
Cried out in distress.
With no thought of becoming Kyrgyz,
I had the spirits and fairies searched out.
From the city of spirits and fairies,
Sixty cunning sorcerers
I expressly ordered brought.
Paying them gold and jewels by the pood each month,
Thinking, ‘This way he will not come to Beijing;
Manas will never see Beijing,’
Dragons, tigers, and many other beasts,
Through magic, I, your Almambet,
Had stationed to guard the road.
